summary: A table of commonly seen header fields in email message headings. It is informational and serves as a handy reference for what these headers are used for.

plainLanguage.summary: The top of an email has many labels like From and Date. This is a cheat sheet that tells what the common ones mean.

what does the reply-to header do
subtitle: A one-stop reference table of the header fields found at the top of Internet mail and Usenet messages.

tldr.problem: Header fields that appear on Internet mail messages and Usenet News articles are defined in many separate RFCs, and some common ones are not defined in any RFC.
tldr.mechanism: The memo lists the headers in one table, grouped by purpose, giving each a short description and a pointer to the RFC that defines it, plus labels such as non-standard, discouraged or controversial.
tldr.outcome: It is an informational aid for people building message systems. It does not specify a standard, and it reflects the state of things in 1996 and 1997.

today: RFC 2076 is an Informational memo and has not been obsoleted or updated. Its table is a snapshot from 1996 and 1997, so treat it as a historical reference rather than a current list of headers.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope of the Table
sections.content:
Many Internet standards and RFCs define headers that may appear on Internet mail messages and Usenet News articles. RFC 2076 collects them in one document as an aid to people developing message systems or interested in Internet mail standards. It draws on RFC 822, RFC 1036, RFC 1123, RFC 1327, RFC 1521 and several others, and adds a few commonly seen headers that no RFC defines.

The memo uses two terms precisely. A heading is the formatted text at the top of a message, ended by a blank line. A header (also called a header field) is one field in that heading: a field name, a colon, and the value or values.

Some things are left out. Attributes of PEM and MOSS only appear inside the message body, so they are not headers in the RFC 822 sense. Envelope attributes used between mail and news servers, such as those of SMTP, UUCP and NNTP, are mainly not covered, and headers used only in HTTP are not included yet.
sections.plainLanguage: It is like one big index card file for all the labels that can be stuck on the top of a letter, so you do not have to hunt through many books.

sections.title: Gatewaying and Usenet Headers
sections.content:
Headers defined in RFC 1327 map X.400 features that were not standardized in Internet mail. Their presence in RFC 1327 means they are recommended for gatewaying messages between X.400 and Internet mail. It does not mean they are recommended for mail wholly within the Internet. At the time of writing (1996) they were not widely implemented or used.

Headers defined only in RFC 1036 are meant for Usenet News. They sometimes show up in mail, either because a message was gatewayed from News to e-mail or because a client handles both. They are not standardized for e-mail and should be handled with caution by e-mail agents.
sections.plainLanguage: Some labels were made for a different kind of mail system, like a newsletter board. When they turn up on ordinary letters, be careful, because they may not mean what you expect.

sections.title: The Labels Used in the Tables
sections.content:
Each entry carries a short remark that tells you how much to trust the header. The memo defines these phrases:

  • not for general usage: defined in RFC 1327 for X.400 gateways, not standardized for exchange between Internet mail systems.
  • not standardized for use in e-mail: defined only in RFC 1036 for Usenet News. Handle with caution in e-mail.
  • non-standard: not specified in any of the referenced RFCs, listed because it often appears. Use is generally not recommended.
  • discouraged: non-standard and known to cause problems, so it should not be generated.
  • controversial: different implementors interpret it differently.
  • experimental: new, to be tried out before entering the IETF standards track, and only to be used if both parties agree.
sections.plainLanguage: Each label on the cheat sheet has a warning sticker, like safe, be careful, or please do not use this one.

sections.title: The Table of Headers
sections.content:
The table has sixteen groups. Each entry gives a description, the header name and the defining RFC. The groups are:

  • Trace information, for example Received:, the trace of MTAs a message has passed, and Return-Path:.
  • Format and control, such as MIME-Version: and Content-Disposition:.
  • Sender and recipient: From:, Sender:, To:, cc:, bcc: and others.
  • Response control, such as Reply-To: and Followup-To:.
  • Identification and referral: Message-ID:, In-Reply-To:, References:.
  • Other textual headers like Subject:, Keywords: and Comments:.
  • Dates and times, quality, language, size, conversion, encoding, Resent-headers, security and reliability, and a miscellaneous group.

Appendix A sorts the headers by the RFC in which they appear, and Appendix B is an alphabetical index.
sections.plainLanguage: The cheat sheet is sorted into drawers: who it is from, who it is to, when it was sent, how it traveled, and so on.

sections.title: Headers With Known Problems
sections.content:
Several entries carry warnings worth knowing. Reply-To: is marked controversial: it is ambiguous because personal replies and group replies may need different addresses, and the author's personal opinion is that it should be avoided except in special cases. Newsgroups: can appear in e-mail with two contradictory meanings.

Apparently-To: is inserted by Sendmail when the original message has no To: recipient. The memo calls this not quite proper, since MTAs should not modify headings except to insert Received lines, and it can wrongly reveal Bcc recipients. Content-Length: is discouraged because using it in transmission can cause robustness and interoperability problems. Precedence: is non-standard, controversial and discouraged.

The memo also notes that From without a colon is used in the Unix mailbox format to separate messages in a file, and its information should not be used to find an address for replies.
sections.plainLanguage: A few labels cause confusion, like a sign that points two ways at once. The cheat sheet warns you about those.

sections.title: Status of the Memo
sections.content: RFC 2076 is Informational. It states that it does not specify an Internet standard of any kind. The author intended to keep updating the document after publication and asked readers to report headers that should be included but are missing. The table reflects what the author found in the listed RFCs, not a ruling on what mail software must do.
sections.plainLanguage: This is a helpful guide, not a rulebook. Nobody has to follow it, but it is handy to look things up.

viz.caption: THE REMARKS USED IN THE TABLE

items.title: not for general usage
items.text: Defined in RFC 1327 for X.400 gateways.

items.title: non-standard
items.text: Seen in practice, but in no referenced RFC.

items.title: discouraged
items.text: Known to cause problems; do not generate.

items.title: experimental
items.text: To be tried out; use only if both sides agree.

references.text: RFC 822, source of many mail headers such as From:, To: and Date:.
RFC 1036, source of the Usenet News headers.
RFC 1327, source of the X.400 gatewaying headers.
RFC 1521, source of the MIME headers.
